End-to-end capacity-constrained policy learning · project report

Code review, corrections, and a re-run experiment suite

Everything from this working session in one place: what the code did wrong and how it was fixed, the experiments re-run afterwards on three datasets, two standalone studies, and the two figures prepared for the paper. Charts are interactive — pick an experiment and a metric, and switch methods on and off.

What this is

The project learns treatment-allocation policies from observational data when each treatment arm has a long-run capacity budget. Rather than the classic two-stage pipeline — fit outcome models, then price capacity with an LP — the outcome model is trained end-to-end against an inverse-propensity-weighted estimate of policy value, with the dual capacity prices re-solved at every step as an implicit function of the model. That makes it a bilevel program, differentiated with the implicit function theorem.

Five method families are compared throughout:

  • F — end-to-end through the non-convex softmax Lagrangian (scipy L-BFGS-B forward, IFT backward).
  • G / Gs — end-to-end through the convex log-sum-exp dual; G via a CVXPYLayer, Gs via the same scipy + IFT machinery.
  • Alt — block-coordinate: prices refreshed periodically and held fixed, dropping the chain-rule term through them.
  • S2-* — the two-stage baseline (Tang et al. 2024) with linear / lasso / tree / kNN / DR / MLP outcome models.
  • random, treat-all — reference policies, one of them deliberately capacity-infeasible.

The three results that matter

What was done

  1. Reviewed and refactored the codebase — deduplicated ~2,000 copy-pasted lines, added 16 numerical tests, and proved the refactor changed nothing (bit-identical outputs against the pre-refactor code on all three datasets). Details in the Code cleanup tab.
  2. Fixed four correctness issues, the important one being a train/eval leak in both real-data loaders. Details in Corrections.
  3. Re-ran every experiment afterwards — 170 cells, one SLURM job each, 10 seeds per point. Explore them under Results explorer.
  4. Added two studies the paper had no data for: how τ trades policy sharpness against feasibility, and how runtime scales in the number of treatments.
  5. Produced two publication figures, in Paper figures.

One number: Deployment-Adjusted Policy Value

A method is not its validation value: what matters is what people receive once the policy runs against real capacity. DAPV scores exactly that, with no arbitrary weights:

DAPV(κ) = (1 − u)·Vserved + u·V0 − κ·W

Value is what the deployed assignments deliver (ground truth on the synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets; IPW on the real ones). Feasibility needs no weight at all — an infeasible policy mechanically loses value through the queue: u is the fraction of arrivals never served, priced at the no-intervention outcome V0. Delay enters through W, the mean wait over all arrivals, priced at κ per waiting period. κ is the index's only parameter, so instead of choosing it we put it on the axis — every reader applies their own delay-aversion, and the crossovers are reported, not tuned. Values are normalized per dataset (random = 0, best-at-κ=0 = 1) so κ reads as "fraction of the value-at-stake per waiting period", and the combined index is the unweighted mean over all six datasets. Per-decision compute is identical across methods (an argmax over |T| scores), so runtime differences live in training only — see the scaling study.

Temperature study — τ trades sharpness against feasibility

G's inner optimum satisfies E[πt] = bt exactly on binding arms, so it is feasible-in-expectation by construction. F's is not, and the gap it opens is controlled by τ. Switch views to see the pure objective effect, then the same two methods after real training.

When does end-to-end help? — the regime map

Both dials of the Adult semi-synthetic problem, swept jointly: how nonlinear the true effect surface is (λ, left to right) against how tight the capacity constraints are (top = tightest). Each cell is the mean over seeds of the difference in ground-truth policy value between end-to-end F and the best two-stage baseline at that configuration — blue where end-to-end wins, red where two-stage does. The hypothesis, registered before running: end-to-end pays off in the tight-and-nonlinear corner and has nothing to offer when constraints are slack or the surface is linear — which would also retro-explain LaLonde (slack) and Criteo (two arms, mild surface).
